preamble: Solutions to six across and three down clues are people who are deemed 17, historically, and are not further defined.

clue.text: Elegant young bird putting bloke off

indicators.note: to put something off is to remove it, so these letters are taken away from the word in front

parts.note: a young bird, especially a young fowl
Ken is a typical man's name, so it stands for any bloke

explanation.surface: A smart fledgling bird is driving away an unwanted man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' completes the indicator 'putting ... off'. Setters often use a common first name such as KEN, LEN or DES for 'man' or 'bloke'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic describes stylish, fashionable appearance, a direct synonym of elegant.

clue.text: Enzyme operates in a strange way

indicators.note: doing something in an odd manner means the letters come out in an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A biochemist remarks that some enzyme behaves oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads naturally as a sentence about enzyme behaviour; the verb is really the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A protease is a specific kind of enzyme that breaks down proteins, so this is an example.

clue.text: Paid less? Keeps doing nothing here

indicators.note: something that keeps another thing holds it inside, so the result lies within the words before

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A worker who is paid less decides to stop working altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes it look like a complaint about wages; the two opening words are simply the container for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle means inactive, not working or occupied; an adjective matching the phrase about inactivity.

clue.text: Ex-football manager in on task for rebuilding

indicators.note: rebuilding means putting the parts back together in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former football boss is brought in on the job of rebuilding a team.
explanation.walkthrough: Ron Atkinson was a well-known English football manager, of Manchester United among other clubs, later a TV pundit.
explanation.definitionFit: Ron Atkinson managed several English clubs and has since retired, matching a former football boss.

clue.text: Skilful, admitting each failure

indicators.note: to admit is to let someone in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: deft means skilful, nimble
EA is a standard abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: Even a skilful person sometimes has to own up to every failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitting' reads as confessing, but here it means letting in.
explanation.definitionFit: A defeat is a loss or a failure to win, so the noun is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Drug in grown-up rave is contaminating influence

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside, between the surrounding letters

parts.note: a grown-up is an adult
to rave is to rant, talk wildly
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Ecstasy at an adults' rave party is seen as a corrupting influence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rave' suggests a dance party, which fits the drug; here it is the verb meaning to rant. The drug sits inside the pair of words joined together.
explanation.definitionFit: An adulterant is a substance added to make something impure, so it contaminates whatever it enters.

clue.text: What sounds like grim yarn

indicators.note: something that sounds like a word is spoken the same, so the spelling may differ

parts.note: grim can mean harsh and pitiless

explanation.surface: A dark, grim tale is described as a yarn, a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' tempts as a story to go with 'grim', but it means thread. Crewel is a thin worsted wool used in embroidery.
explanation.definitionFit: Crewel is a fine two-ply woollen thread used for embroidery and tapestry work.

clue.text: Important people, not female stars

indicators.note: saying not to something removes it from the word being built

parts.note: in British slang, faces are well-known or influential people
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A list of VIPs that pointedly excludes female celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Female stars' looks like one unit, but 'stars' is the definition at the end. 'Faces' is British slang for notable people, as in well-known faces.
explanation.definitionFit: Aces are people who excel at something, the top performers, just as stars are.

clue.text: Duck in animal group

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a herd is a group of animals
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A duck has wandered into a group of other animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Herod the Great was the king of Judea at the time of Jesus's birth; the preamble makes him a GREAT and gives no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Herod the Great, client king of Judea under Rome, is one of the rulers the preamble calls Great.

clue.text: Article on love by Ancient Greek

parts.note: the definite article
love is zero in tennis, written as O
Doric was a dialect of ancient Greek

explanation.surface: An essay about love written by a classical Greek author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient Greek' looks like a writer but it is a language. Theodoric the Great was king of the Ostrogoths and ruler of Italy around 500 AD.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodoric the Great, Ostrogothic king of Italy, is one of the historical figures the preamble calls Great.

clue.text: Bizarre act by the man touring Ireland

indicators.note: something bizarre is strange and out of order, so these letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: touring means going all the way round, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: the man is he
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A man puts on a strange performance while travelling around Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine the Great was Empress of Russia in the 18th century; the preamble supplies her title.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine the Great, Empress of Russia, is one of the historical figures the preamble calls Great.

clue.text: Women wearing garlands

indicators.note: something being worn is wrapped by what is worn, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: leis are Hawaiian flower garlands
W is an abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: Women decked out in flower garlands, as at a Hawaiian welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis is an old English form of Louis; Louis I of Hungary is known as Lewis or Louis the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis the Great, the fourteenth-century king of Hungary and Poland, is one of the preamble's Great rulers.

clue.text: Form of heating brought to French city

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for central heating
Arles is a city in Provence, southern France

explanation.surface: A heating system is being installed in a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles the Great is Charlemagne, King of the Franks and first Holy Roman Emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlemagne's name literally means Charles the Great, the Frankish emperor crowned in 800.

clue.text: Like a budgie maybe of a hundred — old!

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
aged means old

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a pet budgie seems to live to a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation suggests a centenarian bird, but 'a hundred' is just the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Budgerigars are usually kept in cages as pets, so a budgie is a typical example of something kept enclosed.

clue.text: Strict adherence to narrow understanding limits real manoeuvring

indicators.note: manoeuvring means moving things around into new positions, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sticking rigidly to a narrow reading restricts genuine room to act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limits' reads as the verb of the sentence, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Literalism means taking words in their most exact, basic sense, ignoring metaphor or wider meaning.

clue.text: Yorkshire cheek is heard? One will help man stop flapping

definitions.text: One will help man stop flapping

indicators.note: something heard is taken by the ear, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: a tyke is a nickname for a Yorkshireman
lip means cheek, insolent talk

explanation.surface: Someone's Yorkshire impudence is overheard, alongside a tip on keeping things from flapping.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'tyke lip' runs together as the answer. Tyke is a long-standing nickname for a person from Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie clip fastens a man's necktie to his shirt so it does not blow about or dangle loose.

clue.text: Nag driving son away

indicators.note: driving something out removes it, so that letter disappears from the word
completes the phrase about driving off, confirming that something is sent out of the word

parts.note: to nag is to pester
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A nagging parent ends up driving their son out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away' completes the indicator 'driving ... away'. Peter the Great was the Tsar who modernised Russia around 1700.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter the Great, Tsar and first Emperor of Russia, is one of the preamble's Great historical rulers.

clue.text: Big gun engineers imported

indicators.note: imported goods are brought in, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: gat is old slang for a gun
RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

explanation.surface: Army engineers have brought in a large artillery piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big gun' looks like one unit, an artillery piece, but 'Big' is the definition on its own. This is the word the preamble's theme rests on.
explanation.definitionFit: Great is a plain synonym of large in size, as in a great expanse.

clue.text: Only three bridge players currently?

parts.note: with only three at a table of four, one seat has no player
the bridge players are named by compass points; the absent one here is West, W

explanation.surface: A bridge club asks whether it has only three players at the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the four players are named by compass points; three players means one seat is empty, so 'no W' describes the table.
explanation.definitionFit: Now and currently both mean at the present time, so the adverbs are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Plant with strange odour, very strong

parts.note: W is an abbreviation for with

indicators.note: strange means odd or unusual, so these letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud or strong

explanation.surface: A plant that gives off a weird and powerful smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a pungent plant; 'very strong' is the music notation for fortissimo.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodruff is a small woodland herb with white flowers, smelling of hay when dried; it is one kind of plant.

clue.text: A very big order for sailors

parts.note: taken as written
vast means very big

explanation.surface: A huge purchase order placed on behalf of a ship's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a purchase, but it is a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Avast is a nautical command telling sailors to stop or hold what they are doing.

clue.text: Stupid subaltern's a mug

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled and senseless, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A foolish junior army officer is called a mug, an easy dupe.
explanation.walkthrough: A subaltern is a junior army officer; a mug is a gullible fool. Albertus Magnus, Albert the Great, was a 13th-century German theologian and scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnus is Latin for great, so Albertus Magnus is literally Albert the Great, matching the preamble's theme.

clue.text: Illustration of Indian city with dull border

indicators.note: a border runs round the edge, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: dim means dull, not bright
Agra is the Indian city of the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: A picture of an Indian city framed by a drab border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dull' is both a source of letters and part of the phrase saying it forms the frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a simplified drawing showing how something works, a kind of illustration.

clue.text: Cockney semi-embarrassed

parts.note: semi means half, which a Cockney says without its H
an embarrassed face goes red

explanation.surface: A Londoner who is half embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech, the working-class London accent, drops the initial H. Alfred the Great was the 9th-century king of Wessex who fought the Vikings.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred the Great, Anglo-Saxon king of Wessex, is the only English monarch traditionally called Great.

clue.text: See 21
Commander to be removed initially in time of revolution

parts.note: OC is Officer Commanding, a military commander
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A commanding officer is about to be ousted during a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removed' looks like a deletion signal, but it simply contributes its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 is known as the October Revolution, so the month was a time of revolution.

clue.text: Food that sounds dreadful to some?

indicators.note: a thing that sounds like another is spoken the same, though spelt differently

parts.note: awful means dreadful; in some accents the two words sound alike

explanation.surface: A dish that some diners find simply horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To some' hedges the sound match, which works only in certain accents; it also suits the surface, as many people dislike this food.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal means the edible internal organs of animals, such as liver and kidneys, which are eaten as food.

clue.text: Something round to toss up? Maybe, once

definitions.text: Something round to toss up? Maybe, once

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the order is flipped

parts.note: to lob is to toss
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Asking what round object might be tossed, perhaps in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: an old coin that could be tossed. In the wordplay the round letter is added to the toss before the whole thing goes up.
explanation.definitionFit: An obol was a small silver coin of ancient Greece, a round thing one might flip in former times.

clue.text: For the old girl I cater with difficulty, losing pounds

indicators.note: doing a thing with difficulty suggests struggle and disorder, so these letters are rearranged
losing something means it goes missing, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to feed an elderly woman while cutting costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old girl' looks like one phrase, but 'For the old' is the definition and 'girl' is raw material. The letter dropped comes out before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Geriatric relates to the care of elderly people, as in geriatric medicine, so it describes what is meant for them.

clue.text: Beer being served with ten in bar

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Beer is being served to a group of ten in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, which fits the beer, but it is a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: An axle is a metal rod or shaft on which wheels turn, so it is a kind of bar.

clue.text: Go unhurriedly, avoiding a penalty

indicators.note: avoiding something means leaving it out, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: to coast is to move along without effort or hurry
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to take things slowly so as to stay out of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A penalty' looks like one phrase, but the article is the letter left out and 'penalty' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cost can mean a loss or sacrifice paid for something, as in at the cost of, which is a penalty.

clue.text: Series of deliveries is difficult, we hear? One's put too much in

definitions.note: with 'One's' the clue reads as 'one has overstuffed'; the definition is the verb phrase

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled

indicators.note: what we hear is taken by the ear, so the sound counts and the spelling can change

parts.note: is difficult becomes 's tough, contracted

explanation.surface: A tricky spell of cricket bowling, and someone who has packed something too full.
explanation.walkthrough: Deliveries suggests post, but in cricket a delivery is a ball bowled and six make an over.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstuff is to cram too much into something, such as a cushion or a suitcase.

clue.text: Behold Scottish island, wasting time

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning behold, look

indicators.note: wasting something means losing it, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: Uist is an island in the Outer Hebrides
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Look at a Scottish island where people idle the hours away.
explanation.walkthrough: Louis XIV of France was called the Great as well as the Sun King; Uist (North and South) lies in the Western Isles of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis XIV, the Sun King, was also hailed as Louis le Grand, one of the preamble's Great rulers.
